CausalChain: Fibrotic liver disease → Increased ECM stiffness → Activation of integrin β5/FAK/MEK/ERK signaling in resident macrophages → Polarization into M2‐like, immunosuppressive TAMs → Secretion of TGF-β, LOXL2 and ECM remodeling enzymes → Further increase in matrix stiffness → Reinforcement of tumor-promoting microenvironment
Hypothesis: A self-reinforcing mechanotransduction loop exists in fibrotic livers, whereby increased matrix stiffness drives the polarization of TAMs toward an M2 phenotype, and these M2 TAMs, in turn, secrete factors that further stiffen the extracellular matrix and promote hepatocellular carcinoma. Interrupting the integrin/FAK-based mechanotransduction in TAMs will disrupt this loop, repolarize macrophages to an M1 phenotype, and suppress liver cancer progression.
Abstract: Tumor‐associated macrophages (TAMs) in liver cancer exhibit dynamic phenotypes that are influenced not only by soluble factors but also by biophysical cues from the tumor microenvironment. In the fibrotic liver, increased matrix stiffness is known to affect macrophage polarization; however, a potential self‐reinforcing loop whereby mechanical forces modulate macrophage behavior and, in turn, further alter the extracellular matrix remains underexplored. Here, we propose that increased matrix stiffness in fibrotic livers activates integrin‐mediated mechanotransduction in Kupffer cells and recruited monocytes, driving their polarization toward an immunosuppressive M2 state. M2 TAMs then secrete factors such as transforming growth factor‐β (TGF‐β), lysyl oxidase–like 2 (LOXL2) and other extracellular matrix remodeling enzymes that augment matrix stiffness and create a favorable niche for hepatocarcinogenesis. Disrupting this mechanotransductive feedback loop through inhibition of integrin/FAK signaling may shift the balance of TAM phenotypes toward the pro‐inflammatory, anti‐tumorigenic M1 state and thereby enhance antitumor immunity. In this hypothesis, we explore the potential of combining mechanotransduction‐targeted therapies with existing immunotherapies to break the vicious cycle driving liver cancer progression.
